title: Scalable and Differentiable Point-Cloud Registration Using Maximum Mean Discrepancy
claim: A two-stream attention network processes paired inputs with cross-attention, fuses them, and branches into separate heads that each predict a global parameter.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right, crossing arrows between two CAB streams, then four branches
description: A single left-to-right block diagram of a neural architecture. At left, two inputs X and Y each enter a row of rounded boxes labeled CAB_1, CAB_2, ..., CAB_N. Diagonal crossing arrows between the rows show that each stream feeds the other's next block, which is cross-attention. Dotted arrows mark the elided middle layers. Both streams then converge on a single box, SAB_c. From there four arrows fan out to four rows. The top row is SAB_o then Lin_o, giving output v, w. The other three rows are SAB then PMA then Lin, giving r, t and ℓ. Everything is black-and-white line art with rounded rectangles and LaTeX subscripts. The eye goes first to the crossing arrows on the left, then to the branching fan-out on the right.
caption: Set transformer architecture for Neural MMD-Reg. Alternating CABs process source and target point clouds, followed by concatenation and set attention. PMAs predicts global parameters, with the scale parameter constrained via a softplus nonlinearity.
abstract: We present MMD-Reg, a novel correspondence-free approach to point-cloud registration that is differentiable and has linear computational complexity in the number of points. We model registration as a nonlinear least-squares problem based on the Maximum Mean Discrepancy, approximated using random Fourier features. The resulting objective can be solved efficiently with standard methods such as Levenberg-Marquardt, and the solution is differentiable via the implicit function theorem. This allows MMD-Reg to be used as a differentiable optimization layer within end-to-end trainable models, supporting registration under challenging conditions such as poor initial alignment and partial overlap. We demonstrate this Neural MMD-Reg formulation by integrating the layer with a set transformer, training the resulting model in supervised and unsupervised settings, and comparing its performance against recent learning-based methods. We also evaluate standalone MMD-Reg, comparing its accuracy and scalability against widely used non-learning-based registration methods.
